html:
The Vietnamese alphabet, chữ Quốc ngữ, is the Latin based script in which Vietnamese is written today. It was created by European missionaries in the 1600s and became the national script only in the twentieth century.

Portuguese Jesuits such as Francisco de Pina worked it out in the early 1600s to learn the language and preach. They used Portuguese spelling habits and added marks for Vietnamese tones. The French Jesuit Alexandre de Rhodes built on their work and in 1651 printed in Rome a Vietnamese, Portuguese and Latin dictionary, the first major book in the script.

For two more centuries Vietnamese scholars wrote in Chinese characters and in chữ Nôm, a script adapted from them, in which classics such as The Tale of Kiều were written. Under French rule the colonial government promoted the Latin script and ended the old examinations in 1919. Vietnamese nationalists then embraced it as a tool for mass literacy, because it was far easier to learn. After 1945 it was used in literacy campaigns across the country.
sum: The Vietnamese alphabet, chữ Quốc ngữ, is the Latin based script in which Vietnamese is written today. It was created by European missionaries in the 1600s and became the national script only in the twentieth century.
